column1: # Where each Latin noun's gender in lex-la.tsv was read.
# The tooltip prints a noun's gender beside it, and its word page prints it
# in the Gender row and the page's description. On 2026-10-06 every noun was
# read against its own entry in Lewis & Short, from the Perseus text, which
# tags the gender in an entry's head. The first gender an entry gives is the
# headword's, except where a parenthesis about another form comes first —
# solum's collateral sŏlus, m., lūx's old forms "also used as m.", sāl's
# plural sales, m. — so those were read by eye, as was every homograph and
# every word given inside another word's entry.
# Seven disagreed with the seed. hostis, mīles, canis (dog and hound), mūs
# and bōs are "comm." in Lewis & Short, the gender c, which the tooltip
# prints as "common", and the seed gave all six m; bōs's head goes on
# "generally masc. in prose", which says how the gender is used, not what it
# is. And locus is "i, m. (… plur. loci, single places; loca, places
# connected with each other, a region)", which the seed gave n, the gender of
# the plural it wove. A row carries one gender for both its forms, so the
# plural is locī now, whose gender is the headword's: a reader is told
# masculine under locus and under locī, and neither is false.
#   ls:<key>   Lewis & Short, by the entry's key in the Perseus text: no
#              macrons, j for a consonantal i, a digit for a homograph (os1
#              the mouth, os2 the bone, canis1 the dog).
# A word Lewis & Short gives inside another entry cites both: serpēns at the
# end of serpo, patria under patrius, marītus under the adjective maritus,
# respōnsum under respondeo. Two headwords are filed under another spelling,
# autumnus under auctumnus ("correctly aut-") and iūsiūrandum under
# That test requires every noun in lex-la.tsv to have a line here with the
# same gender, every line to cite its own entry, and every line to have a
# noun. It cannot tell an entry somebody read from one somebody typed.
